cards.front: A segment tree answers a range query by combining how many precomputed chunks?

options.text: Exactly two, one from each half
options.response: That is the shape of a single split, but a range usually straddles more than one boundary on the way down.

options.text: At most O(log n) of them
options.response: Yes. The walk splits only where the range demands it, and it can only demand a split once per level.

options.text: All n leaves in the range
options.response: That is the brute-force scan the tree exists to avoid — if it read every leaf it would cost the same as no tree at all.

options.text: One, because the tree stores every range
options.response: Storing every possible range would need O(n squared) nodes. The tree stores a fixed set of chunks and combines them instead.

cards.front: Why does the query walk stop descending at some nodes?
cards.back: Because that node's range is fully inside the query range, so its stored answer is already the answer for that whole chunk. Descending further could only re-derive what it already holds.

cards.front: Updating one element changes how many nodes in the tree?

options.response: The leaf's ancestors all summarise it, so leaving them stale would make every range containing that element wrong.
Yes. That is one node per level, which is why an update is O(log n) rather than O(n).
Most nodes summarise ranges that do not contain the changed element, so nothing about them changed.
